title: How Apparel Buyers can Control Midseason Hanger Substitutions
description: Read article about Learn how apparel buyers can manage hanger substitutions with samples, defined approvals, carton traceability, receiving checks, and closure rules during shortages. and more articles about Textile industary at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Labelled photos, complete samples, agreed acceptance checks, and garment tests help buyers judge whether a substitute hanger part affects fit, grip, or fabric marking.
A defined release should state the styles, quantities, destinations, approval number, packing instructions, carton range, and receiving checks covered by the temporary exception in clear order records.
markdown:
A hanger substitution can start with a short supplier message. The approved clip is out of stock, and an alternative is available before the packing date. The proposed clip fits the same hanger body. The factory wants to know whether it can go ahead. The buyer has to decide whether the change will keep the order on schedule while preserving the way the garment looks and behaves after packing.

That decision becomes easier when the buyer can trace a temporary approval to the styles, quantities and shipments it covers. A useful exception record answers four questions. What changed? Where does it work? Which cartons contain it? When does the approval end? The same method applies when a shortage affects a hook, a coating or the hanger body itself.

## Ask for a Side by Side Sample

Ask the supplier to identify the exact component that is unavailable, the approved version, the proposed substitute and the earliest delivery date for each option. Request a side-by-side photo with both versions labelled. Use it to spot differences that matter for the application, such as a different jaw face on a clip, a taller hook or a shoulder shape that sits differently under a garment. If the proposed change involves a coating, ask which surfaces will touch the fabric.

Next ask for a complete hanger with the substituted part fitted. Put it beside the approved version and use the same garment on each. Test the styles most likely to expose a problem. For a clip change, that could mean a lightweight skirt that can slip through the pads and a trouser with a thicker waistband that is harder to clamp. Check the fabric after removal under the same light, and reproduce the ordinary handling and packing conditions that the factory or store will use.

Agree on acceptance criteria before comparing the samples. A photograph may answer whether the garment hangs level. A grip or surface-mark question is better assessed using a named garment and a repeatable check. Record the garment style, sample references and what the reviewer observed. Send the same result to the people responsible for quality, sourcing and packing.

## Approve a Defined Release

Imagine a hypothetical order for 12,000 garments across three styles. The substitute passes checks on two trouser styles. It leaves a visible impression on the lightweight skirt. The buyer authorises up to 4,000 substitute hangers for the two trouser styles in the first shipment. The third style keeps the original hanger or waits for a different option. The numbers describe the limit of that release and should be replaced with the quantities and order lines on the actual purchase order.

Put the decision where people will use it. The order amendment should reference the substitute and the approval number. The packing instruction should list which garment styles may use it and which must be put aside if the approved stock runs out. Quality control needs an example or an annotated image of the replacement. If inspectors open several cartons, they should be able to tell whether each carton was packed against the normal instruction or the exception.

A buyer can accept a compromise explicitly. A different hook shade might be permissible on a shipment for stockroom use and visibly inconsistent on a set of coordinated front-of-store rails. The written approval can distinguish the destinations. That gives the supplier and the warehouse a shared instruction and leaves the final merchandising decision with the buyer.

## Make the Exception Visible at Receiving

Once packing begins, link the exception to a lot or a carton range. Agree on how it will appear in the packing list and receiving instructions. Ask the receiver to compare the first cartons of the affected range with the approved sample or its reference photos. If a carton has an unexpected component, preserve its identifier before segregating it. That makes the next check specific to a shipment and helps the factory trace which instructions were used.

GS1's Global Traceability Standard describes recording data about events such as packing, shipping and receiving. A buyer can use that principle with whatever order and warehouse systems are already in place. The practical requirement for this decision is that a receiving team can connect the carton it opens to the component approval that applies to it. A supplier's email saying it used the approved alternative cannot do that job on its own.

## Close the Approval When the Shortage Ends

Set an end condition while approving the substitute. It could be a purchase-order line, a maximum quantity or a shipment cutoff. Then ask the supplier to reconcile how many alternatives it used and whether any remain. If the original part is available again, confirm which shipment restarts the normal specification. If the alternative should become the permanent version, review it for the wider assortment and issue a new revision through the usual approval process.

The record can be short. Give it an owner and include the reason for the change, the two sample IDs, the eligible garment styles, the receiving identifier and the end condition. The next time the factory asks whether an available part can be used, the answer can move quickly from the sample room to the right cartons without silently changing the specification for the next order.
